content: The definitions of indicators are consistent across frameworks. However, there are variations in how the numerator or denominator is calculated. Some indicators are reflected as either a numerator or denominator in other frameworks. Condom programming addresses both the demand and supply aspects of increasing the use of male and female condoms. This includes fostering a supportive social and political environment for condom use, promoting consistent and correct condom use among men, women, and transgender individuals, and ensuring the acceptability, availability, and affordability of condoms and condom-compatible lubricants. Condom promotion and distribution strategies vary depending on the target population. For example, in the general population or among clients of sex workers, condom use is often promoted through social marketing campaigns that direct individuals to retail outlets selling condoms, often at subsidized prices. For adolescents or young people, additional sales venues may be included. For key populations such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, and transgender individuals, condoms may be distributed free of charge or at subsidized prices in high-risk settings (e.g., brothels, entertainment venues) or through peer outreach. Condoms are also distributed through health services, such as family planning, sexually transmitted infection (STI), and HIV services, as well as needle-syringe services and opioid substitution therapy (OST) centers for people who inject drugs, and workplace programs. It is critical to include condoms in service packages for key populations in all epidemic settings and to promote them vigorously for HIV prevention in generalized epidemics. The health sector provides important venues for condom promotion and distribution. Every interaction with clients living with HIV or at risk of acquiring HIV or STIs is an opportunity to advocate for condom use and provide these commodities, ensuring an adequate supply, such as a presumed three-month supply of 30 condoms. The effectiveness of condom programming is measured by the percentage of people who use condoms, particularly during high-risk sexual acts. These measures are typically gathered through population-based behavioral surveys. Indicators define the relevant last sexual act with different types of partners for various population groups. For example, the last sexual act with a non-regular partner among general population adults, the last anal sex act with a non-regular male partner for men who have sex with men and transgender individuals, and the last sexual act with a client for sex workers. To measure and interpret condom distribution indicators, countries must map different distribution mechanisms (e.g., commercial, socially marketed, and free distribution) and assess the extent to which condoms are promoted as part of family planning services and used primarily for contraception rather than high-risk sexual encounters. Every interaction with clients living with HIV or at risk of HIV or STIs is an opportunity to advocate for condom use and provide condoms. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as an additional prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection, as part of a combination HIV prevention approach. This includes comprehensive condom programming and harm reduction for people who inject drugs. An increasing number of countries are adopting policies endorsing PrEP for HIV prevention. In 2019, WHO updated its oral PrEP guidance to include event-driven dosing (ED-PrEP) for men who have sex with men. This four-pill dosing strategy may reduce drug costs, pill burden, and potential toxicity, and improve adherence among individuals who find daily pill-taking challenging. However, it is not currently recommended for other population groups. Many individuals who could benefit most from PrEP belong to key population groups that face legal and social barriers to accessing health services. Therefore, tracking PrEP coverage for these populations through disaggregated indicators is highly recommended. Challenges for adolescents in need of PrEP include legal issues of consent, social and cultural barriers, and infrequent utilization of health services. Monitoring PrEP use and adherence among younger users requires fine age disaggregation (e.g., five-year age bands) to address these programmatic challenges effectively. PrEP services should be integrated with existing services whenever possible and use existing reporting systems. Measurement of PrEP program performance and effectiveness must account for both appropriate and inappropriate discontinuation due to perceived changes in HIV risk. Programs must identify and assess the proportion of individuals who stop PrEP prematurely or are non-adherent. Discontinuation and loss to follow-up, as measured through missed appointments, should be regularly reviewed at the facility level to determine if changes in service approaches, such as enhanced adherence counseling or contact methods, correlate with different rates of continuation. HIV testing services (HTS) encompass pre-test information, HIV testing and diagnosis, post-test counseling, re-testing, and referral and linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. Effective HTS systems focus on population outcomes, such as increasing the proportion of people living with HIV who have been diagnosed, ensuring linkage to treatment, and optimizing linkage to prevention services among HIV-negative individuals at substantial risk of infection. A cost-effective HTS program must prioritize those at the highest risk and vulnerability to HIV acquisition and use available resources for service delivery approaches that best meet the needs of these groups. This includes providing HTS services in both facilities and communities and in settings that minimize stigma and discrimination against people living with HIV and key populations. Community-based testing and self-testing are important components of the HTS service mix and should be accounted for in assessing overall testing uptake, coverage, and linkage to treatment. Repeat testing is critical to ensure that individuals enrolled in prevention programs remain HIV-negative and, when seroconversion is identified, that they are rapidly linked to antiretroviral therapy (ART). The WHO Treat All guidelines emphasize the provision of ART as the foundation of the national health sector response to HIV. Global HIV elimination goals are predicated on the concept of treatment as prevention, combined with evidence-based primary prevention. Monitoring progress in ART scale-up is critical to tracking the overall HIV prevention and treatment cascade, including reductions in HIV incidence and mortality.
